## In this session

-   A very short introduction to **HTML**, **CSS** and **XML**
-   Web basics: how a page actually reaches a browser
-   **GitHub Pages introduction** (approx. 45 minutes)

## The web as an interface

Publication is not the last step after the research; it is part of the argument. What a reader
can see, sort, search and download is a claim about what matters in your data.

## HTML, CSS, XML — the minimum

-   **HTML**: elements, attributes, nesting; structure versus appearance
-   **CSS**: selectors and rules; why separating the two matters for reuse
-   **XML**: the same tree model, but for your own vocabulary — the bridge to TEI next week
-   What "valid" and "well-formed" mean, and why a schema is a data model in disguise

## GitHub Pages

The practical core of the session, and the route to your
[assignment](/contents/assignment.qmd) website:

-   Publishing a repository as a website
-   Markdown as source, HTML as output
-   Static site generators, briefly — what Quarto (this site) or Jekyll do for you
-   Custom domains, and why you probably do not need one
-   **Getting your first page online today**

::: {.callout-tip title="In parallel in the Lab"}
The [DH Lab](https://dhbern.github.io/dh-lab/contents/sessions/06.html) covers APIs the same
week, including the Zotero API — which is one good way to get your bibliography onto the site
you build here.
:::
